Iran on Friday dismissed Saudi Arabia's accusations that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, with its Foreign Ministry offering to mediate between Riyadh and the Yemeni group to help ease tensions.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh.
Baqaei said Tehran "has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities" and remained prepared to use "all its capacities for this purpose at the request of both sides".
The Houthis are part of Iran's so-called "Axis of Resistance," which also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq, all united in opposing Israel.
Tehran has repeatedly denied directing Houthi operations, saying the Yemeni group acts according to its own interests.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets in recent weeks, including vessels in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week.

articles.title: Houthis’ diverse arsenal fuels renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have built a diverse missile and drone arsenal that allows them to sustain attacks against Saudi Arabia and strategic maritime targets, raising concerns...
articles.full_text:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have built a diverse missile and drone arsenal that allows them to sustain attacks against Saudi Arabia and strategic maritime targets, raising concerns about the duration and intensity of the renewed conflict.
Since early September, the group has struck key oil infrastructure and airports across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s airport, which has been targeted 20 times, according to the supplied account. It has also attempted, unsuccessfully, to strike the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The renewed hostilities followed a Saudi bombardment of Sanaa’s airport in July aimed at preventing a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital, ending a four-year truce.
April Longley Alley, a Yemen specialist at the Washington Institute think tank, described the subsequent exchanges as a strategy of reciprocal escalation.
“The Houthis framed this campaign as blockade for blockade, airport for airport, escalation for escalation,” she said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and aerial and maritime drones, giving them multiple options for attacking infrastructure and threatening shipping near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a strategic passage linking the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea.
Their weapons come partly from military stockpiles seized when they captured Sanaa in 2014. Others have been smuggled into Yemen as complete systems or assembled locally from imported components, primarily brought in through the Arabian Sea, said Niranjan BS, a strategic weapons analyst at Jane’s.
According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Military Balance database, the group operates several medium-range ballistic missiles, including systems derived from Iranian designs such as the Kheibar Shekan.
Its shorter-range weapons include the Asef anti-ship missile, derived from Iran’s Khalij Fars missile family, according to the Wilson Center think tank.
The Houthis also possess cruise missiles from Iran’s Quds family. The Quds-4 variant is believed to have a range of about 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles), the Wilson Center said.
Their drone arsenal includes the Waeid-1 and Waeid-2, local copies of Iran’s Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 one-way attack drones, respectively, Niranjan said.
This combination allows the group to vary its attacks and threaten targets at different distances, complicating efforts to neutralize its capabilities.
Iran has provided critical military assistance to the Houthis, particularly through missile and drone technology, according to the Middle East Institute.
In a report, the institute said components manufactured in Iran are smuggled into Yemen by small boats, container ships or across the border with Oman before being assembled locally.
However, analysts caution against portraying the Houthis as a force that simply follows Tehran’s orders.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli analyst specializing in Iran, said the Houthis viewed themselves as partners of Iran rather than proxies.
Iranian personnel linked to the Quds Force, the foreign operations arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, maintain a presence in Yemen and advise the group, Citrinowicz said at a recent conference in Paris. But he said they do not decide Houthi military operations.
In June 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned a man in China suspected of links to the Houthis, accusing him of playing “a key role in procuring materials that enable Houthi forces to manufacture advanced conventional weapons inside Yemen.”
The Houthis have survived years of conflict and sustained air campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the United States and Israel, leaving them experienced in operating under military pressure.
Longley Alley said their ability to withstand previous bombardments suggested that further strikes might not quickly end the confrontation.
“We need to remember with the Houthis that they have withstood punishing air campaigns before, from the Saudis, from the Americans, and from the Israelis,” she said.
“This is a battle-hardened group, and they have much less to lose than the Saudis.”
She added that the Houthis likely believed they could sustain the conflict longer because they were accustomed to absorbing attacks.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks violate terms of rapprochement with Iran - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia says Houthi attacks violate terms of rapprochement with Iran  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has publicly accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis to attack the kingdom, saying it violates a 2023 diplomatic deal it reached with Tehran to smooth over relations.
"We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, told journalists on Friday, in a rare public statement.
Krimly’s comments mark the first public signal that the war in Yemen has put pressure on Riyadh’s ties to Tehran.
Krimly said that the Houthis’ attacks were a breach of a March 2023 rapprochement that was brokered by China under which Saudi Arabia and Iran resumed diplomatic relations. At the time, the agreement was seen as a sign of China’s successful foreign policy. Beijing has good ties with both Tehran and Riyadh.
“[Iran] continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and in violation of its commitments in the Beijing agreement,” Krimly said.
The agreement was generally understood to include a commitment from Tehran to restrain the Houthis in support of a United Nations-backed ceasefire.
Saudi Arabia has faced multiple attacks since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, putting pressure on the delicate rapprochement the two countries struck. Saudi Arabia even joined the US in launching some strikes on Iran earlier this year in retaliation, although it later pivoted to mediation.
Despite the tensions, Saudi Arabia has maintained diplomatic engagement with Iran.
Pressure
Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan held a phone call with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi this week. Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia’s ambassador to Iran publicly attended Araghchi’s sister’s funeral.
But the kingdom is now reeling from intense Houthi missile and drone strikes that have targeted civilian infrastructure including airports, oil facilities and the corporate headquarters of Aramco.
The Houthis garnered support in the Muslim world for attacking vessels linked to Israel and the US after 7 October 2023, when Israel responded to a Hamas-led attack by launching a war on Gaza, deemed a genocide by the UN, human rights groups and genocide scholars. But the group’s attacks on civilian sites in Saudi Arabia have sparked backlash.
Video footage from the Houthis' Saturday strike on Riyadh airport showed Umrah pilgrims absorbing a strike that killed at least 13 people and severely wounded hundreds more.
Saudi Arabia led an intervention into Yemen’s civil war in 2015. The kingdom launched a devastating bombing campaign against the Houthis that contributed to what the UN called the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.
In 2022, Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose biggest backer is Saudi Arabia, reached a ceasefire with the Houthis. The agreement ushered in a fragile truce that endured even during US and Israeli strikes on the Houthis.
The Houthis have received arms, training and intelligence from Iran.
The war in Yemen erupted again after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Houthi officials from landing. Middle East Eye reported that Iranian, Syrian and Hezbollah military advisors were on board, along with weapons systems.
The Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping as a result, and launched a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast last month, which the kingdom and its Yemeni allies have struggled to counter. They have also launched hundreds of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Trump: Israel helping Saudi Arabia against Houthis, normalization closer than ever - Israel National News
articles.summary: Trump: Israel helping Saudi Arabia against Houthis, normalization closer than ever  Israel National News
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump said Friday that Israel has been providing assistance to Saudi Arabia in its confrontation with the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, while expressing optimism about the prospects for diplomatic normalization between Jerusalem and Riyadh.
Speaking with reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked whether Saudi Arabia should accept Israeli assistance in its campaign against the Houthis.
"Yeah, I do. I think they will. Israel has been very helpful to Saudi Arabia," the President responded.
Trump's remarks suggested that cooperation between Israel and Saudi Arabia has continued despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations between the two countries.
Asked whether Saudi Arabia's potential entry into the Abraham Accords was once again under consideration, Trump indicated that the prospects for an agreement had improved.
"Yeah, I think so. Maybe more than ever. The Abraham Accords is one of our great achievements. But Saudi Arabia is very happy to have Israel's support and our support," he said.
The United States has sought to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords, the normalization framework established during Trump's first administration.
Israel and Saudi Arabia appeared to be making progress toward a US-mediated diplomatic agreement before Hamas launched its October 7, 2023, terrorist attack against Israel.
Following the massacre, the Saudi government suspended the American-backed normalization initiative, leaving the proposed agreement unresolved.
Trump has subsequently linked the prospect of closer US-Saudi nuclear cooperation to Riyadh's willingness to establish official diplomatic relations with Israel.
In July, Washington and Riyadh announced a nuclear cooperation agreement known as a 123 Agreement.
Two days after the agreement was signed, Trump told reporters that Saudi participation in the Abraham Accords was a requirement for proceeding with the arrangement.
“I just say that in order to do it, they have to be a member of the Abraham Accords, which have been very successful. But it's time now that they do it," Trump said at the time.
His latest comments indicate that he continues to view Saudi-Israeli normalization as a central objective of American diplomacy in the Middle East, alongside cooperation against Iranian-backed forces in the region.
(Arutz Sheva-Israel National News' North American desk is keeping you updated until the start of Shabbat in New York. The time posted automatically on all Israel National News articles, however, is Israeli time.)

articles.summary: At least 5 killed in Houthi attack on Yemen’s presidential palace in Aden  Al JazeeraYemen's Houthis hit palace in Aden, coalition details attacks on Saudi infrastructure  ReutersYemen’s government says Houthis fired two missiles at Aden airport  Al JazeeraHouthi Missiles Strike Government Headquarters in Yemen  The New York TimesIran-aligned Houthis target Yemeni presidential palace, prime minister remains unharmed  CNN
articles.full_text:
At least five people have been killed in the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Yemen’s port city of Aden after Houthi missile strikes.
Yemeni health minister says five people were killed and 16 others injured in the Houthi missile attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden on Thursday.
The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.
The government says the prime minister and other officials are safe, but two of his bodyguards were killed in the attack.
Plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the vicinity of the palace.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported earlier on Thursday that there were explosions near the palace.
The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.
“This is an indication that the escalation is going to intensify between both sides,” Mawry said, adding that fears are now growing inside the country of “an all-out civil war” that could potentially drag in other regional powers besides Saudi Arabia.
The attack in Aden came as fighting between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and Saudi-backed forces intensified in Taiz, which is effectively under siege by the Houthis.
Controlling Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the broader Taiz governorate, in the southwest of the country would ensure control over the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait for either side.
Forces allied with the Yemeni government said they are repelling a Houthi attack on Dhubab airport.
The pro-government Homeland Shield Force said in a statement that they are, along with the Southern Giants Brigades, securing the airport in the coastal city of Dhubab in Taiz governorate.
Aid agencies say the escalating violence in Taiz is pushing the healthcare system towards breaking point.
On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,
The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.
“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.
Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.

articles.title: At UNSC, Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reaffirms support for kingdom's security - Dawn
articles.summary: At UNSC, Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reaffirms support for kingdom's security  Dawn
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON: Pakistan on Thursday strongly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s civilian and economic infrastructure, reaffirming its support for the kingdom’s security and right to self-defence amid escalating regional tensions.
Speaking at a United Nations Security Council (UNSC) debate on the Middle East, Pakistan’s acting Permanent Representative, Ambassador Usman Jadoon, said, “These attacks must cease immediately.”
He reiterated Islamabad’s support for efforts to secure a peaceful settlement in Yemen.
Pakistan also backed the UN special envoy’s efforts to resume dialogue aimed at achieving a comprehensive and lasting peace in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has, in recent days, come under sustained attack, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the deadliest in years, as the war with the Houthis dramatically escalates.
Yemen’s civil war reignited in July after a UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The conflict in the country has caused what the UN calls one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
The Saudi-led coalition has fought the Houthis since 2015 after they seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa and forced out the internationally recognised government from the city, until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
Concern expressed over Gaza
In the same session, Pakistan joined the call for halting settler violence in the West Bank and abandoning attempts to annex occupied Palestinian territory.
“In the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, settlement expansion, particularly the E1 project, threatens to sever Palestinian territorial contiguity. Settler violence, demolitions, land seizures and forced displacement are entrenching annexation and dismantling the foundations of peace,” Jadoon said.
“All settlement activities must cease […]; settler violence must be halted; and accountability ensured.”
The E1 plan was greenlit by Israel last year and would further separate east Jerusalem, occupied and annexed by Israel and predominantly inhabited by Palestinians, from the West Bank.
Jadoon added that the international support for a two-state solution to the Palestinian issue must be accompanied by concrete measures to preserve Palestine’s territorial integrity and viability.
“The two-state solution remains the internationally agreed framework and the indispensable foundation for just and lasting peace,” he said, adding that Resolution 2803, the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, and the New York Declaration provided mutually reinforcing frameworks for advancing that objective.
“Pakistan supports their full and good-faith implementation,” he added.
He also condemned Israeli incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque and demanded respect for the historical and legal status quo of the holy sites.
Regarding Gaza, Pakistan expressed concern over continued ceasefire violations, Palestinian deaths and restrictions on humanitarian access.
Jadoon warned that the approaching winter threatened to worsen the suffering of families living amid destruction without adequate shelter or essential services.
He called for the Gaza ceasefire to be fully upheld, humanitarian assistance to be delivered unhindered and at scale, and recovery and reconstruction to proceed without delay.
Pakistan also stressed the need to support the work of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, and demanded the release of withheld Palestinian revenues to enable the Palestinian Authority to fulfil its responsibilities.
Jadoon rejected forced displacement and any attempt to fragment Gaza and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, which he said constituted a single territorial unit.
He called for a “credible, time-bound and irreversible” political process to end the Israeli occupation and establish an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian state on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital.
Jadoon concluded that lasting peace in the Middle East would remain out of reach as long as the occupation continued and the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination remained unfulfilled.
“Pakistan remains committed to advancing dialogue and diplomacy in the region to help de-escalate tensions, resolve differences and promote lasting peace and stability,” he said.
The Palestinian representative, Deputy Permanent Observer Majed Bamya, said Israel continued to kill Palestinians despite the ceasefire and questioned what he described as unequal international responses to Israeli and Palestinian casualties.
“If violence is an impasse, as we are often told, and I believe it is, how can Israeli militarism be justified while Palestinian pacifism is demanded?” he asked.
Bamya said Israel had squandered the international sympathy that followed the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, through the killing of Palestinians, including children, and the destruction of entire multigenerational families.
He said more than 1,000 Palestinians had been killed over three years in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, while Israeli settlers and soldiers continued to perpetrate violence.
He called for Gaza and the West Bank to be reunited under the Palestinian Authority, with one government, one legal system and one security authority.
“We are either sovereign states, equal in rights and duties, sharing security and prosperity, or warring parties forever,” he said, adding that “occupation must end”.
France’s ambassador, Jerome Bonnafont, also called for an end to Israeli settlement expansion, warning that the E1 project, settler violence and financial pressure on the Palestinian Authority were fuelling instability.
“The unchecked expansion of settlements—including the E1 project—the clear trajectory toward annexation, the systematic and unpunished acts of terror committed by settlers, and the financial strangulation of the Palestinian Authority all fuel instability, including for Israel itself,” he said.
Britain echoed the criticism of Israeli settlement policy. Ambassador Sarah MacIntosh demanded an immediate halt to the E1 project, withdrawal of the relevant tender and an end to settlement expansion.
“The Government of Israel must ensure compliance with its obligations under international humanitarian law and remove the current restrictions on this critical aid,” she said, referring to humanitarian assistance for Gaza.
The United States defended President Donald Trump’s comprehensive Gaza peace plan, endorsed by Security Council Resolution 2803 (2025), saying its success depended on Hamas disarming and relinquishing its weapons.
The UN’s acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, warned that the ceasefire remained extremely fragile, with Israeli military operations continuing to cause Palestinian casualties.
Citing Gaza’s Ministry of Health, he reported approximately 1,500 Palestinian fatalities since the ceasefire, including more than 320 children and 140 women.
“During my visit to Gaza on Sunday, I witnessed that, for Palestinians living along the Yellow Line, the ceasefire exists in name only,” he said.
Alakbarov warned that winter would deepen the humanitarian crisis, with an estimated 950,000 people living in areas at medium or high risk of flooding and more than 4,000 buildings being used as shelters at risk of collapse.
He called for the full implementation of the Gaza peace plan, including the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups, withdrawal of Israeli forces, deployment of the international stabilisation force and transfer of transitional governance responsibilities to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
He said the ceasefire must become the foundation for genuine recovery and a lasting political settlement, paving the way for two states living side by side.

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are at War with Saudis for own Reasons, not as Iran Proxy - Informed Comment
articles.summary: Yemen’s Houthis are at War with Saudis for own Reasons, not as Iran Proxy  Informed Comment
articles.full_text:
By Laurent Bonnefoy, Sciences Po
(The Conversation) – A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.
As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics, I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.
Houthi narratives
The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.
It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied. At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.
What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.
A belated return to war
When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.
But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them, in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.
Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims, was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.
Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.
An earlier airport bombing
During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.
The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes. Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.
From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.
After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.
The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.
Saudi’s Houthi blowback
The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.
Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.
These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.
With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia, with consequences extending to the global economy.
This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
Photo by Mauro Lima on Unsplash 
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.
It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.
Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.
Laurent Bonnefoy, CNRS research fellow, Center for International Studies, Sciences Po

articles.full_text:
European Union leaders called on Israel to immediately reverse plans to expand illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and warned businesses against bidding for construction contracts, citing serious legal, economic and reputational risks, according to a statement issued Friday following a two-day summit in Brussels.
In conclusions adopted at the Oct. 15-16 European Council meeting, EU leaders condemned Israel's continued expansion of illegal settlements and escalating violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank.
The leaders specifically demanded that Israel abandon plans for new settlement construction in the E1 area, a controversial development project that threatens to further fragment Palestinian territory and undermine prospects for a viable Palestinian state.
The European Council also urged companies and financial institutions to refrain from participating in construction projects linked to illegal Israeli settlements, warning that involvement could expose them to serious consequences under international law.
"It reiterates that businesses should not bid for construction contracts for E1 or other settlement developments," the declaration said.
The statement highlighted the legal, economic and reputational consequences facing businesses and financial institutions involved in illegal settlement construction, including the risk of serious violations of international law.
EU leaders also expressed grave concern over the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, reiterating their opposition to Israeli policies that undermine Palestinian rights and regional stability.
Separately, the European Council criticized U.S. sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court (ICC), urging Washington to reverse the measures.
The leaders reaffirmed the bloc's commitment to defending the court's independence and ensuring its continued access to financial services and other resources necessary for its operations.
The EU said it remained prepared to take steps to protect the ICC from measures that could obstruct its work.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are illegal under international law. The International Court of Justice reaffirmed this position in its July 2024 advisory opinion, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territories unlawful.

articles.title: Russia, US eye new joint projects as diesel deal faces sanctions hurdles
articles.summary: Russia and the United States are preparing to unveil new economic initiatives, including potential nuclear-powered data centers, as Washington seeks to overcome sanctions-related o...
articles.full_text:
Russia and the United States are preparing to unveil new economic initiatives, including potential nuclear-powered data centers, as Washington seeks to overcome sanctions-related obstacles to a recently announced Russian diesel deal, a senior Kremlin envoy said Friday.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, said Moscow and Washington were exploring several areas of collaboration that could move forward even before the war in Ukraine ends.
Speaking at the Russian Energy Week conference in Moscow, Dmitriev said discussions included joint data center projects that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
He said additional initiatives would be announced soon, describing the diesel agreement reached between U.S. President Donald Trump and Putin as a potential model for broader economic cooperation.
The developments come as the two countries navigate a complex sanctions landscape that threatens to complicate efforts to expand commercial ties.
Dmitriev said the U.S. Treasury Department had approached the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which he heads, for assistance in resolving payment difficulties linked to the diesel agreement.
According to Dmitriev, Washington asked the fund to facilitate transactions and address technical obstacles that could hinder implementation.
The RDIF would work to ensure payments were processed efficiently and reached their intended recipients, he said.
The agreement, announced by Trump last week, would allow Russian diesel to reach U.S. and international markets in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of November's U.S. midterm elections.
Lower energy costs have become a key political priority for Trump, but the arrangement has drawn sharp criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and raised questions about the future of U.S. sanctions targeting Russian oil.
Implementing the deal would require Washington to ease certain restrictions, including measures imposed by the Trump administration itself.
Dmitriev acknowledged that overlapping sanctions had created considerable uncertainty over how the agreement could proceed.
"There are so many layers of sanctions piled on top of one another that everyone has become confused," he said, adding that U.S. officials were examining ways to remove the relevant restrictions.
He said discussions were already underway on possible sanctions relief, suggesting that Washington was actively seeking a workable solution.
However, Dmitriev warned that a separate U.S. sanctions and tariff measure, known as the Graham Act, could effectively shut down broader investment cooperation between the two countries.
The legislation, introduced by the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, is intended to intensify economic pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Dmitriev argued that the measure would undermine potential Russian-American business ventures and limit both countries' ability to cooperate in stabilizing global energy markets.
He maintained that economic engagement could proceed alongside diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, with the diesel agreement potentially opening the door to additional projects.
The discussions underscore Moscow's push to revive commercial ties with Washington despite continuing tensions over Ukraine and extensive sanctions imposed on Russia.
While Dmitriev expressed optimism about further agreements, the proposed initiatives remain subject to significant legal and political hurdles as Washington weighs economic cooperation against its existing sanctions framework.

articles.title: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz - CNBC
articles.summary: One Singapore ship was sunk, but here's why others are still transiting the Strait of Hormuz  CNBCTwo ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles amid surge in attacks  ReutersIran Guards say oil tanker exploded after hitting mine in 'unauthorized' route through Hormuz  The Times of IsraelShips in Strait of Hormuz still face "indiscriminate attacks," maritime monitor warns  CBS NewsShip attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports ...
articles.full_text:
Commercial vessels are likely to continue navigating the perilous Strait of Hormuz despite the sinking of a Singapore-flagged container ship this week, as strong demand for Middle Eastern energy and lucrative shipping opportunities keep some operators willing to brave escalating attacks, maritime experts said.
The latest attacks on two Singapore-flagged container ships have heightened concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints. But analysts say the incidents are unlikely to bring remaining shipping activity through the Strait to a halt, even as major container lines largely stay away.
Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said shipping companies were likely to continue seeking opportunities to transit the strait despite heightened security threats.
“I don’t see in the short term, that Singapore flagged ships or Singapore shipping companies would necessarily avoid taking the transit if there is an opportunity,” Koh told CNBC.
His comments follow attacks on two Singapore-registered container ships, GFS Pride and GFS Giselle, this week. GFS Pride sank after being struck by a projectile and catching fire, while GFS Giselle was damaged. Crew members from both vessels were reported safe.
Crossings through the Strait of Hormuz fell to 131 in the week ended Oct. 14, from 176 the previous week, according to maritime analytics firm Kpler, although the decline cannot be attributed solely to the latest incidents.
Dimitris Ampatzidis, maritime risk and compliance manager at Kpler, said the attacks underscored Iran’s continuing ability to threaten commercial vessels, with the risks extending beyond oil and gas transportation.
Koh said shipping companies around the world have continued looking for opportunities to navigate the Strait since the conflict erupted, with some operators prepared to accept higher risks and costs.
Strong demand for oil, particularly from Asia, continues to provide an incentive for tanker operators to transport energy supplies from the Persian Gulf, even as security threats complicate voyages.
Some operators may be willing to take their chances even if doing so involves paying a premium, Koh said.
Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan offered an example of how higher oil prices could make voyages through Hormuz commercially worthwhile despite the dangers.
Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit last week, Balakrishnan recounted a conversation with an unnamed Gulf counterpart who said his country was earning more from oil exports than before the war by operating a so-called “Hormuz shuttle” involving about 20 very large crude carriers.
The vessels were effectively self-insured against attacks, according to the official’s account, with higher crude prices making the voyages financially worthwhile despite the risks.
“Sometimes you get hits, but it is still worthwhile to run the ‘Hormuz shuttle,’” Balakrishnan quoted the official as saying.
Despite the risks, vessels continue to transit the Strait, reflecting its commercial importance, particularly for energy shipments to Asian markets, Ampatzidis said.
However, further attacks could deter more operators from making the passage, with the impact likely to differ depending on vessel type and individual companies’ assessments of the risks, he added.
The Singapore Shipping Association also played down the prospect of a broad withdrawal of commercial shipping from the region, suggesting operators would instead adapt to changing trade conditions.
“Rather than signalling a broad withdrawal from the region, these developments are more likely to result in adjustments to trading patterns as markets respond to shifts in the supply and demand of goods and energy,” said association president TS Teo.
Shipowners would continue weighing commercial considerations against security developments and crew safety when making operational decisions, he added.
While some operators remain willing to transit Hormuz, much of the global container shipping industry has already adjusted its networks to avoid the strait.
Jayendu Krishna, a director at Drewry Maritime Advisors, said none of the major container shipping lines had resumed services through Hormuz since suspending operations following the outbreak of the war in February. Only some regional operators have continued sporadic services, generally using smaller feeder vessels.
That means the immediate impact of the latest attacks on container shipping could be limited, he said.
However, a further escalation into the Gulf of Oman could pose a more serious threat to regional supply chains, particularly if it disrupts alternative ports like Khorfakkan in the United Arab Emirates and Oman’s Sohar that have become critical gateways for cargo entering Gulf countries.
“If the Gulf of Oman became a zone of kinetic activity, a significant part of supplies to the Gulf countries would be cut off, since Khorfakkan and Sohar have been a lifeline for them,” Krishna said.

articles.title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary  The GuardianA Gaza war documentary sparks outrage in Israel  NPRNAZA film review — Israeli accounts of assault on Gaza make brutally hard viewing  Financial TimesNetanyahu demands probe into sources for award-winning Gaza film NAZA  Al JazeeraI survived Gaza's horrors. I watched NAZA to learn how Israeli soldiers live with it  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.
NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.
In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.
British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.
Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”
The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.
The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.
The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”
The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.
The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.
When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.
The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.
Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

The U.S. State Department and The Washington Post on Friday condemned violence following an attack by illegal Israeli settlers on American photographer Heidi Levine while she was covering the Palestinian olive harvest in the occupied West Bank, with Washington calling for an investigation and accountability for those responsible.
"The Department of State is aware of these reports. We are greatly concerned when any American is harmed overseas and stand ready to provide all appropriate consular assistance," a State Department spokesman said in an emailed statement to Anadolu Agency (AA).
"The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance," the spokesman added. The department added that the Trump administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans, and that Washington remains in regular dialogue with partners on improving stability and security in the West Bank.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the spokesman said. The statement did not mention Israeli occupiers.
"This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” the newspaper’s Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement.
"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist,” he added.
Murray said the Post is "relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe,” but stressed: "We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.”
Palestinian rights group Al-Baydar said Levine was assaulted by the occupiers in the presence of Israeli troops, and was taken to Al-Istishari Hospital.
Levine was one of two journalists injured on Friday in attacks by Israeli occupiers across the Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorate, which also left at least 12 Palestinians wounded, many of them farmers harvesting olives, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, the Civil Defense and Al-Baydar.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said this week it had documented at least 136 attacks linked to the olive harvest season by Israeli forces and occupiers since the beginning of October.
The olive harvest is a vital source of income for thousands of Palestinian families in the West Bank, where farmers face growing attacks and restrictions on access to their land during the season.
Attacks by Israeli forces and occupiers against Palestinians and their property across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, have intensified since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.

articles.title: Israeli ad firm under fire over harvesting data to deploy spyware
articles.summary: Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech exploited a vast commercial ad network to collect personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, accordin...
articles.full_text:
Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech exploited a vast commercial ad network to collect personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, according to an investigation published Thursday by Canadian cybersecurity watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant.
The operation used advertising infrastructure for covert surveillance, allowing operators to identify potential targets, track their online activity and deliver spyware while evading detection. Confiant described the campaign as highly sophisticated, citing its anti-interception measures and precise targeting capabilities.
The investigation linked the operation to Israeli spyware company Candiru, which has been blacklisted by the United States and rebranded as Integrity Labs, and surveillance vendor Intelos. The companies allegedly exploited commercial advertising inventory across major platforms, including Google, Beeswax and Russia's Yandex, to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
"The core finding is the weaponization of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterized by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting," Confiant said in its findings.
Citizen Lab described the campaign as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through online advertising, a method researchers called "AdFection."
Devices belonging to staff members at international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through weaponized ad placements, which operated silently without visible pop-ups or suspicious links.
Discover-Tech operated a specialized system called Controlium that turned routine commercial advertising auctions into a surveillance system.
After analyzing 4 billion bidding records, researchers found that the company distributed ads across nearly 200,000 unique websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS devices in dozens of countries over a four-month period.
"Discover-Tech serves roughly 10 million ad impressions a day, and each one feeds an identity graph built from device fingerprints, IP addresses, advertising IDs, and often the publisher’s own first-party cookies," Confiant said.
Investigators found that the ads routinely collected user session cookies, authenticated login tokens and personal identifiers directly from publisher websites, exfiltrating the data even when European Union privacy regulations prohibited processing without consent.
Citizen Lab also identified an affiliated threat actor, dubbed Dark Cartographer, that used Discover-Tech's infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across mobile telecommunications providers. The group matched digital advertising identities with phone numbers to identify mobile subscribers on a large scale.
Geographic data revealed sharp spikes in traffic that researchers said pointed to deliberate intelligence operations rather than ordinary commercial advertising campaigns.
Palestine emerged as the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech served nearly 2% of all digital advertisements, peaking at roughly 10% on April 7. One in every 36 Android ads in the territory originated from the firm.
Surveillance traffic also reached sensitive administrative and institutional networks, including the Armenian Prime Minister's Office, international organizations, judicial agencies, universities and defense organizations.
Investigators detected targeted connections to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56% of observed activity, followed by the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain and other countries.
Following disclosure of the joint investigation, Google, the European advertising association IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi cut off Discover-Tech's access to their digital advertising systems.

Israel has halted commercial shipments into Gaza for a second consecutive day, cutting off a vital source of food and other essential supplies as Palestinians face worsening hardship and prepare for winter.
Israeli authorities blamed the suspension on Palestinian merchants protesting taxes imposed by Hamas, but Gaza's private truckers union disputed that account, accusing Israel of imposing the restrictions itself.
The suspension threatens to disrupt supplies of fresh food, meat and winter clothing in the war-ravaged territory, where nearly 2 million people depend on goods entering through Israeli-controlled crossings.
With access to Gaza tightly restricted, any interruption to commercial deliveries risks driving up prices and leaving families struggling to afford basic necessities.
Humanitarian organizations warn that aid deliveries alone cannot meet the population's needs.
While aid agencies generally supply staples such as flour, private merchants play a crucial role in bringing in perishable foods, including fruit and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body responsible for coordinating humanitarian affairs in Gaza.
A functioning commercial market is also essential to keeping prices within reach for families who have already endured years of war, displacement and severe shortages.
"The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people," said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council. "The markets need to be functioning."
COGAT announced the suspension Wednesday, saying it had followed a decision by Palestinian merchants a day earlier to stop coordinating shipments because of Hamas-imposed charges and alleged threats against importers.
"We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas's taxation mechanism and threats against them," said Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, COGAT's deputy spokesperson. "The merchants don't want to bring goods into Gaza."
The agency said no private-sector vendors had attempted to bring goods into the territory since merchants notified Israeli authorities Tuesday.
But Nahed Sheheiber, head of Gaza's private truckers union, rejected Israel's explanation, saying Israeli restrictions, rather than a voluntary decision by merchants, were responsible for the suspension.
"The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments," Sheheiber said. "The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza's merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions."
Following COGAT's announcement, the union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to raise concerns that Israel was using fees charged by the ministry as a pretext to restrict commercial supplies.
Sheheiber said the ministry had asked merchants to pay 10,000 Israeli shekels, or about $3,226, for each truck entering Gaza. During the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab said the payment was not a tax but a donation intended to help pay civil servants in the territory.
The competing accounts leave uncertainty over the immediate cause of the halt, while the consequences for Gaza's already fragile supply network could be severe.
Israel has long accused Hamas of imposing fees on imported goods to finance its operations. However, the suspension places the immediate burden on Gaza's residents, who rely on shipments approved by Israeli authorities for much of their food and other essential supplies.
It also remains unclear whether aid agencies will be permitted to increase deliveries to offset the loss of commercial goods.
COGAT estimates that Gaza's population of roughly 2 million requires about 250 truckloads of goods each day. That figure is substantially below the minimum of 600 trucks per day stipulated under a ceasefire agreement brokered by the United States a year ago.
The suspension comes despite signs of improvement in Gaza's food security earlier this year. The world's leading authority on food insecurity reported that conditions had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but remained at crisis levels, with most families still unable to obtain enough food.
The assessment warned that "even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains," underscoring the risks posed by the interruption of commercial deliveries.
For families already struggling to secure food, the loss of another supply channel could mean higher prices, fewer choices and greater difficulty obtaining essential goods as temperatures fall.
The restrictions also highlight Gaza's dependence on access controlled by Israel. Merchants coordinate with suppliers outside the territory, but their shipments must undergo Israeli military inspections before entering. That system leaves the enclave particularly vulnerable to decisions that interrupt the movement of goods.
The broader humanitarian crisis stems from the war that began Oct. 7, 2023, following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel that killed about 1,200 people in Israel and took 251 hostages.
Israel responded with an extensive bombardment and ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
The ministry says more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the cease-fire took effect.
Women and children account for about half of those killed, according to the ministry.

articles.title: Trump rules out nukes against Iran, keeps strike threat alive
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying the United States did not need them, while warning that Washington could launch further strikes aga...
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying the United States did not need them, while warning that Washington could launch further strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities as he predicted the war would end soon.
In an interview Thursday with Newsmax, Trump addressed reports that his administration was considering deploying the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iran, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump stressed that the weapon was conventional, not nuclear, describing it as an extremely powerful bomb.
“The mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “This is just an extremely large bomb.”
He repeated the distinction, saying the weapon was a conventional munition despite its destructive capacity.
Asked directly whether he would use nuclear weapons against Iran, Trump dismissed the possibility, saying Washington had no need to resort to them.
“No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to,” he said.
However, Trump left open the possibility of additional American attacks on Iran's nuclear infrastructure, specifically mentioning a suspected underground facility known as Pickaxe Mountain.
“Now, we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there,” Trump said. “We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast.”
The site is suspected of being part of Iran's nuclear program, and Trump's remarks suggested that Washington was considering further action to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Trump indicated that such an operation would not necessarily involve American ground troops. Asked whether U.S. forces would be deployed on the ground, he said he did not expect that to happen.
“No, I don't see that. I don't see that,” he said.
The president also warned that the United States might need to carry out additional military operations if it withdrew before ensuring Iran could never acquire nuclear weapons.
“We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said, suggesting that the prospect of future strikes would remain if Washington believed its objectives had not been achieved.
Despite signaling the possibility of further attacks, Trump predicted that the conflict would end in the near future, citing negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
“The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon,” he said.
“One way or the other, it'll end very soon. And oil will go dropping like a rock, and gas prices as well.”
Trump's comments linked his expectations for an end to the conflict with the prospect of falling energy prices, which have been a major concern amid the fighting and uncertainty surrounding oil supplies.
He also claimed that Iranian officials had asked Washington to halt American and Israeli military operations, although he did not provide further details about the alleged request.
“They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them,” Trump said.
His remarks offered little detail about the status of the negotiations, the issues under discussion or the conditions that might lead to a cessation of hostilities.
Trump's prediction of a swift end to the war came alongside his warning that the United States remained prepared to strike additional Iranian nuclear facilities if necessary.
The administration's approach, as outlined by the president, combines diplomatic engagement with the threat of continued military action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
Trump also addressed his relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose government has been involved in the military campaign against Iran alongside the United States.
Asked whether he trusted Netanyahu, Trump gave a blunt response.
“I don't trust anybody, honestly,” he said.
He reiterated his position, adding: “In the world of politics, I don't trust anybody.”

articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia says it thwarted a missile strike on Medina, and other Middle East developments
The Saudi-led coalition says it has thwarted a missile attack on Medina and another in eastern Saudi Arabia
The Saudi-led coalition says it has thwarted a missile attack on Medina and another in eastern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis deny responsibility for the Medina attack, despite previously targeting Saudi airports and oil facilities. The conflict intensified after the Houthis seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait last month. Meanwhile, Turkey's Defense Ministry states that deploying Turkish forces to Saudi Arabia requires parliamentary approval. In Gaza, an Israeli strike killed one man, continuing a pattern of violence despite a ceasefire with Hamas. In Syria, a court sentenced five people over last year's coastal violence.
The Saudi -led coalition fighting the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels said Thursday it has thwarted a missile attack on the holy city of Medina as well as another attack in the eastern part of the kingdom.
Meanwhile, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed one man, hospital officials said.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Thursday. Read our full coverage here.
Houthis deny responsibility for new attack on holy city
The Saudi-led coalition confirmed in a statement that it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile over the province of Medina, but notably did not assign blame for the attack.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree denied carrying out the attack. The rebel group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.
Medina is where the Prophet Muhammad established the Muslim community, while Mecca is where the prophet was born and received his revelations. It's viewed as the holiest city in Islam.
The international airport in the capital, Riyadh, has suspended service because of Houthi attacks. Dozens of flights also were canceled or delayed at Jeddah airport, according to Flightradar24, a flight tracking platform.
Earlier Thursday, Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over Eastern province, a major oil-producing region.
The latest conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transport of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, has been trying to retake them.
Deploying Turkish forces to help Saudis needs parliament approval
Turkey’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that a mutual defense pact between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, as well as any deployment of Turkish forces under the agreement, requires parliamentary approval.
In a statement, the ministry also indicated that no final decision had been made on the type of assistance Turkey might provide to Saudi Arabia.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, and Turkish officials say it is expected to be ratified by parliament in the coming days. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and other officials have ruled out the deployment of combat troops, stressing that the pact is purely defensive.
Israel carries out deadly strike in Gaza
An Israeli strike north of Gaza City killed one man on Thursday morning, according to officials at Shifa Hospital.
Israel’s military said it struck a “terrorist” in the area, without elaborating.
The strike came over a year after a ceasefire deal was reached between Israel and the Hamas militant group, a period during which Israel continued to launch deadly strikes on the enclave.
More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire was reached in October last year, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Syria sentences 5 over last year’s coastal violence
A Syrian court on Thursday sentenced two people to death and three others to prison terms over their roles in last year's sectarian violence in the country’s coastal region.
In March 2025, loyalists of ousted Syrian President Bashar Assad attacked members of the new government’s security forces in areas where a large segment of the country’s Alawite religious minority live. The government’s counterinsurgency spiraled into widespread violence in which hundreds of civilians — most of them Alawites — were killed.
Two members of the pro-Assad groups were sentenced to death and a third to 12 years in prison. Two members of the security forces received prison terms.
EU-GCC meeting has been postponed
The European Union announced in a statement that the joint meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council members set for Oct. 24 in the Saudi capital has been pushed back.
No new date has been set for the gathering that would bring together leaders from the 27 EU economies and the Gulf states of Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates
The EU did not explain why the meeting was being delayed, but the security situation in Riyadh remains uncertain following back-and-forth strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

articles.title: EAM Jaishankar to host counterparts from UAE, US in Mumbai next week - India's News.Net
articles.summary: EAM Jaishankar to host counterparts from UAE, US in Mumbai next week  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
New Delhi [India], October 16 (ANI): External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar will host counterparts from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and the United States (US) in Mumbai on October 19-20, while also attending celebrations marking the 250th anniversary of US independence as a Guest of Honour, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) stated on Friday.
Responding to a question from ANI during a bi-weekly media briefing in New Delhi, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal stated that the meeting between EAM Jaishankar and his UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, would provide an opportunity to review all dimensions of bilateral cooperation, alongside discussions on the situation in West Asia, as well as global and multilateral matters.
Elaborating on the schedule, Jaiswal stated, when asked about EAM Jaishankar's upcoming meetings, 'On 19th and 20th October 2026, the External Affairs Minister will host in Mumbai the Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of the UAE, His Highness Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, for an official visit. On 20th October, the External Affairs Minister will hold talks with the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and attend the celebration of the 250th anniversary of the independence of the United States of America as the Guest of Honour.'
He further added, 'The visit of the UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister will be an opportunity to review all facets of bilateral cooperation under the India-UAE Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The two delegations will assess and take forward initiatives in the areas of energy, trade, investments, fintech, defence and connectivity. There will naturally be an opportunity also for a detailed exchange on the situation in West Asia, as well as on global and other multilateral issues.'
Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan's upcoming visit to India follows EAM Jaishankar's recent official visit to the UAE from October 14-16, during which he held discussions with the country's leadership and attended the Raisina Middle East event.
The MEA spokesperson noted that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's forthcoming visit to India would provide an opportunity for both nations to review bilateral ties and explore avenues to further strengthen the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.
Jaiswal stated, 'In so far as the visit of the Secretary of State is concerned, this forthcoming visit will provide an opportunity for both sides to review India-US relations and discuss ways to further strengthen the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership that we have with the United States. Discussions are expected to cover key areas of our bilateral cooperation, including energy, trade, investment, defence, critical emerging technologies and other areas of mutual interest. The two sides will also exchange views on regional and global developments. The visit will provide an opportunity to sustain the high-level engagement between the two countries and advance our shared priorities.'
According to the US State Department, Rubio will travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar next week for talks encompassing 'enhanced energy cooperation'. During his visit, Rubio is scheduled to meet senior government officials to consolidate the US-India strategic partnership, share perspectives on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation. Additionally, the US State Department confirmed that he would interact with business leaders to foster opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation.
Addressing queries regarding the selection of Mumbai as the venue for EAM Jaishankar's bilateral engagements, Jaiswal responded, 'It has been the practice for the last decade or so that we have hosted foreign dignitaries outside Delhi. To just give you some examples, the Prime Minister hosted the Prime Minister of Spain in Baroda. He hosted Chancellor Merz in Ahmedabad. Prime Minister of Mauritius was hosted by him in Varanasi, and the External Affairs Minister hosted the SCO Foreign Ministers Meeting in Goa. He hosted the Foreign Minister of Botswana in Kevadia in Gujarat, and the External Affairs Minister also hosted the Heart of Asia Conference in Amritsar. So, that was just to give you a few examples of the meetings of leaders, of dignitaries that have happened outside of Delhi.' (ANI)
