articles.title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements - BBC
articles.summary: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements  BBCChinese FM tells Herzog that Israel should stop ‘forced establishment’ of settlements  The Times of IsraelChina tells Israel to stop ‘forced establishment’ of West Bank settlements  Al JazeeraChina pledges continued support for Palestinians, pushes for two-state solution  The Jerusalem PostChina says Israel should stop its 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements &nb...
articles.full_text:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.
Beijing has been a long-standing supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran.
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", he said.
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.
China itself has been accused of trying to dilute its minority populations by encouraging Han Chinese migration to Tibet, which it annexed in the 1950s, and Xinjiang. Beijing rejects those claims, saying its policies promote economic development and social stability.
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has been removed from her position following public scrutiny and President Donald Trump's remarks urging her to reconsider her role, a Wh...
articles.full_text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has been removed from her position following public scrutiny and President Donald Trump's remarks urging her to reconsider her role, a White House official said Friday.
"I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters while departing the White House.
He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"
Fox News, citing a White House official, later reported that Zacharia was "transitioning" out of the role of press secretary.
Zacharia started the job on Monday and held her debut White House briefing on Tuesday.
She had said she received a call about the role of press secretary last Wednesday and got offered the job to succeed Karoline Leavitt last Friday.
Trump later announced her appointment. In his announcement, he described her as an attorney.
Over the last week, the issue of whether Zacharia, a graduate of California's Pepperdine University law school, had actually passed the bar - making her an attorney - came under fire.
On Friday, during a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she did not pass the bar. Anthony Scaramucci served director of communications for 10 days during Trump's first administration.

articles.title: Putin supports Vatican aid initiative for civilians in Ukraine
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin expressed support for a Vatican-led humanitarian initiative to deliver essential supplies to civilians in the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in...
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin expressed support for a Vatican-led humanitarian initiative to deliver essential supplies to civilians in the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, telling Pope Leo during a phone call Friday that Moscow was ready to cooperate.
The Vatican said earlier on Friday that Leo had urged Putin to agree to a truce to allow the entry of first aid and food supplies into the town and to permit a voluntary evacuation of the civilian population.
Russia and Ukraine both accuse each other of blocking supplies to the population of the town which Ukrainian forces want to retake.
"The Vatican’s intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town’s population and to organise vital supplies has been supported," the Kremlin said in a statement.
"It has been agreed to cooperate on this matter."
The surprise notice from the Vatican Friday evening suggested that the recovering pope is still hard at work, despite Tuesday's operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung.
Residents of Oleshky in southern Ukraine are facing a worsening humanitarian crisis with shortages of food and medication as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk denounced on Friday a "desperate" situation in the city, calling on Russia to enable civilians to evacuate.

articles.title: Student protests sweep Europe amid anger over costs of living
articles.summary: Student protests that began with high school blockades in France have spread across Europe, drawing young people into the streets over deteriorating school conditions, teacher shor...
articles.full_text:
Student protests that began with high school blockades in France have spread across Europe, drawing young people into the streets over deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages, rising education costs and a housing crisis that is making it harder to study.
From France and Belgium to Albania, Greece, Spain and Italy, demonstrations have included school occupations, mass marches and protest camps, with some escalating into clashes with police.
Though national grievances differ, the unrest reflects growing frustration among young people who say governments are failing to provide the resources and opportunities they need to build their futures.
The protests began in mid-to-late September, when students in the Paris region, particularly around Creteil, blockaded school entrances with trash bins and makeshift barriers.
They cited missing teachers, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities, including mold, broken toilets and classrooms reaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) during heat waves.
Students have also criticized demanding schedules and Parcoursup, France's university admissions platform, which they say adds stress and uncertainty to the transition to higher education.
The demonstrations quickly spread nationwide, disrupting hundreds of schools. At the peak, more than 200 high schools were reportedly fully closed, while others faced partial closures or interruptions to classes. University students have also joined the movement.
Turnout estimates have varied widely. On Oct. 13, the Interior Ministry counted at least 161,500 demonstrators, while unions estimated participation at nearly 480,000. Other major protest days earlier in October also drew large crowds.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined demonstrators at a blockaded school in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on Oct. 13, arguing that young people were being denied a meaningful role in decisions affecting their futures.
Police conduct has become another flashpoint. A teenager lost a hand in Lens, prompting authorities to suspend the use of stun grenades. Other reported injuries included eye damage and dental trauma, while complaints alleging police brutality were under investigation.
Justice Ministry figures cited in reports put the number of people taken into custody at roughly 6,800 to 8,000, with about 85% to 86% of those detained being minors.
Students, school staff and officers were among those reported injured. Although most marches remained largely peaceful, some ended in clashes involving tear gas, police charges and property damage.
Student unions are demanding an emergency school renovation program, large-scale teacher recruitment, improved schedules and greater student representation. They also want major changes to Parcoursup or its repeal, alongside more nurses, psychologists and career advisers.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced plans to deploy about 3,000 substitute teachers to the hardest-hit schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised a broader plan by the end of October, including consultations and adjustments to the 2027 budget, while citing financial constraints.
President Emmanuel Macron has called for patience and dialogue, but student leaders have dismissed the initial measures as insufficient and vowed to continue demonstrating.
In Belgium, students began demonstrating in early October against tuition reforms, overcrowded classrooms and funding cuts. Some categories of students face fees of up to 1,194 euros for the 2026-27 academic year. Protests spread from Liège to Brussels and other cities, with arrests reported during disorderly demonstrations.
Students also joined a nationwide union-led strike on Oct. 9 against austerity measures. The action drew tens of thousands of participants, while isolated clashes near Brussels Central Station involved water cannon, tear gas and fires.
In Albania, student grievances over university conditions, education costs and limited job prospects have merged with wider protests against corruption and inequality.
Demonstrations have overlapped with the months-long Flamingo Revolution, which opposes a luxury coastal resort project linked to Jared Kushner.
Protests in Tirana escalated into violence, with demonstrators attacking government buildings, banks and infrastructure. Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and batons. Reports described more than 100 arrests at peak points, injuries and significant property damage.
Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign, pledging to address legitimate education concerns while condemning violence and defending his government's push for European Union membership.
In Greece, students set up tents in Athens' Syntagma Square opposite Parliament around Oct. 13 to protest soaring rents and inadequate public housing. Small apartments can cost 500 to 600 euros a month or more, putting accommodation beyond many students' budgets.
Demonstrators are demanding rent controls, more student housing, increased subsidies and better education funding. School sit-ins have also increased over teacher shortages and poor conditions.
In Spain, an indefinite teachers' strike began in the Madrid region on Oct. 14, bringing together educators, students and families under the Marea Verde, or Green Tide, movement. Protesters want increased public funding, smaller classes, higher salaries, reduced teaching hours and more specialized staff. Critics also accuse the regional government of encouraging privatization at the expense of public schools.
In Italy, students have occupied high schools in Turin and Rome, adopting slogans inspired by France as they protest underfunding, deteriorating buildings and rising living costs. Smaller demonstrations elsewhere reflect similar concerns.
Across Europe, the protests expose mounting pressure on public education systems after years of financial constraints, teacher recruitment difficulties and aging infrastructure. Rising rents, energy bills and everyday expenses have compounded those problems, making education increasingly difficult to afford.
Young people also express frustration over their future prospects, arguing that governments are failing to address barriers to education, employment and housing.
France's demonstrations have drawn comparisons with the student unrest of May 1968, although today's movement focuses largely on practical demands involving school conditions, staffing and access to education.
Governments have offered targeted concessions and promised dialogue while emphasizing budget limitations. Yet allegations of police excess, mass arrests and injuries have intensified scrutiny of how authorities respond to youth-led dissent.

articles.title: Cameroon’s rising femicide toll fuels protests, calls for justice
articles.summary: Geraldine Achiah had been married for barely two months when she died in September, leaving behind an 18-year-old son who is struggling to come to terms with her death and demandin...
articles.full_text:
Geraldine Achiah had been married for barely two months when she died in September, leaving behind an 18-year-old son who is struggling to come to terms with her death and demanding justice for what relatives allege was a fatal beating by her husband.
Achiah, an elementary school teacher in her 30s, had encouraged her only child, Courage Abombi, to pursue his dream of becoming a mechanical engineer. He sat for a university entrance exam just one day after her burial.
“My mom died an unexpected and painful death,” Abombi said.
Her death has become part of a growing crisis of femicide in Cameroon, where nearly 70 women have been killed this year in gender-related killings, according to the Ministry of Women's Affairs. The figure exceeds government estimates of at least 50 cases in 2023 and 67 in 2024.
The rising toll has prompted protests in major cities, including Douala and Yaounde, with demonstrators demanding stronger legal protections, more effective investigations and accountability for perpetrators. Many cases remain unresolved, while others go unreported.
Manfred Amambua, Achiah's husband, has denied killing her, police said. He has been charged with murder and is being held in jail awaiting trial. His lawyer was unavailable for comment.
Hospital records obtained by The Associated Press (AP) documented “several bruises on her face and lips” before her death. Ndzana Bienvenu, an officer involved in the investigation, said police had also collected phone footage showing Achiah and her husband after the alleged beating, along with a blood-stained bedsheet.
Her relatives say they want justice not only for Achiah but also for other women who have died in similar circumstances.
“We want justice for our daughter who died a violent death. This was a teacher who imparted knowledge on thousands of young Cameroonians,” said Regina Ngukum, Achiah's cousin.
Activists say femicide in Cameroon is fueled by economic dependence, unequal control over family property and inadequate legal protections in a society where men traditionally hold greater authority within households.
Financial hardship can make it difficult for women to leave abusive relationships, particularly when they have children to support. Some endure violence in the hope that their partners will change, activists say, while stigma and limited resources can make seeking help even harder.
“The current economic situation in the country is not helping matters. With limited resources, many women tend to endure violence in their marriages, hoping that their men will change, which is not usually the case,” Women's Affairs Minister Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa recently told the state broadcaster.
Ondoa described femicide cases in Cameroon as having reached a “cruel” and “alarming” proportion and pledged further government action.
The crisis mirrors a wider global pattern. About 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or other family members in 2024, according to United Nations data.
Activists argue that Cameroon needs stronger laws and a more effective judicial system to prevent gender-related killings and ensure perpetrators face meaningful punishment.
The country's Penal Code criminalizes offenses including rape but does not explicitly define femicide as a separate crime. Cases are therefore handled under broader provisions governing homicide and other violent acts.
Similar approaches are used in many African countries, where killings motivated by gender are generally prosecuted under existing homicide laws, although some governments have taken legal or policy steps specifically addressing femicide.
Cameroon's government is preparing a bill that would establish femicide as a standalone criminal offense while strengthening broader protections against gender-based violence. The proposed legislation is expected to be submitted to parliament for consideration in November.
Activists caution, however, that changing the law alone will not resolve the problems that allow cases to stall or perpetrators to escape accountability.
Carole Grace Mbarga, a Cameroonian activist based in the United States, said investigations and court proceedings can be undermined by intimidation, corruption and procedural errors that may lead to reduced charges or acquittals.
“When investigations drag on, evidence deteriorates, witnesses lose confidence, and families become discouraged,” she said.
Even when convictions are secured, the penalties can fall short of victims' families' expectations. In 2025, a man who pleaded guilty to killing his wife received a suspended five-year sentence and a fine of 52,000 CFA francs, equivalent to about $90.
For activists, such outcomes reinforce concerns that the justice system does not adequately deter violence against women.
Family members and friends gathered in Yaounde for Achiah's burial following her death just two months after her wedding in July.
Her relatives are now waiting for the legal process to take its course while joining a broader movement demanding action against femicide. Thousands of people have taken part in protests in Douala and Yaounde, calling on authorities to strengthen protections for women and ensure that cases are properly investigated and prosecuted.
Laura Sen, one of the protest organizers, said the proposed legislation must be accompanied by efforts to address systemic barriers and improve support for victims of domestic violence.
For women facing abuse, leaving a relationship can be especially difficult when they depend financially on their partners or fear social stigma. Those raising children may face additional obstacles.
Achiah's death has left her son grieving the woman who supported his ambitions and helped him imagine a future beyond their loss.
Abombi said he continues to pray that the legal process will deliver justice for his mother.
“I pray that justice will follow its due course and that her killer will face the law,” he said.
He also described dreams in which his mother returns to comfort him.
“She keeps appearing to me in a dream, consoling me not to despair and that she is still with me,” he said.

articles.title: Macron’s final stretch marred by student protests, police scrutiny
articles.summary: France is facing a growing wave of unrest as high school students protest for better-resourced schools, clashing with police forces accused of using excessive force to suppress dem...
articles.full_text:
France is facing a growing wave of unrest as high school students protest for better-resourced schools, clashing with police forces accused of using excessive force to suppress demonstrations.
The protests, which have spread across the country in recent weeks, have led to mass arrests, hundreds of injuries and mounting criticism of the government’s handling of public dissent.
The confrontations have also exposed tensions within the police, with some officers and their unions accusing the state of putting them in dangerous situations without adequate equipment or clear instructions.
For President Emmanuel Macron, who is due to leave office in May, the unrest is an unwelcome end to nearly a decade in power marked by repeated protest movements and disputes over the use of force against demonstrators.
The latest demonstrations have drawn particular scrutiny because so many of those arrested are teenagers, some of whom have suffered life-changing injuries from weapons used by riot police.
The protests have also attracted public sympathy as France grapples with record poverty and mounting public debt, with students demanding better-funded schools, particularly in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris and other cities.
Yet the demonstrations have also provided cover for violent groups that police say are exploiting the crowds to attack officers, set fires and damage property.
According to government figures, more than 900 police officers and nearly 150 teachers and other school employees have been injured during the unrest. Police say demonstrators have thrown rocks, fireworks and other projectiles at officers, turning some gatherings into violent confrontations.
The competing accounts have intensified a national debate over how France should balance the right to protest with public safety, and whether its security forces are equipped and trained to manage increasingly volatile demonstrations.
Walid Hrar, a police officer and union representative in Paris’ northern suburbs, said France’s long tradition of revolution and civil disobedience helps explain why protests can escalate so quickly.
"This is the country of the French Revolution. Everyone boasts about it, in fact. Some political parties don’t hesitate to say that we need to disobey the law. That’s what Robespierre and other revolutionaries taught us in 1789,” he said.
"France always tends to react rather than anticipate,” he added. "In other words, we’re always going to extremes.”
The response by security forces has become a central point of contention, particularly their use of so-called less-lethal weapons, including grenades, projectile launchers, tear gas and water cannons. Some officers also use riot shields fitted with powerful strobe lights to control crowds.
Critics argue that the deployment of these weapons, combined with inadequate training and poor equipment, increases the risk of serious injuries for both protesters and police.
Jean-Marie Godard, an author who specializes in French policing, said officers were being sent into volatile demonstrations without sufficient preparation.
"We’re sending poorly equipped, untrained public security police officers to violent demonstrations who are likely to become agitated very quickly out of anger and fear,” he said.
Hrar said some officers assigned to crowd-control duties lacked specialized training and protective equipment. He cited uniforms that were not flame-resistant, worn-out helmets and shields unsuitable for the conditions.
"We send them in because we need the manpower,” he said.
He also said officers who lack authorization to use certain riot-control projectiles and grenades can struggle to keep attackers at a safe distance, forcing them into direct physical confrontations.
"So unfortunately we make do,” Hrar said. "You’ll inevitably end up in direct physical confrontation. When that happens, there are injuries on both sides.”
The police union Alliance announced this week that it would file a legal complaint against the state, accusing authorities of endangering officers through unclear and contradictory instructions.
The union said officers had been left "isolated, betrayed, abandoned, exposed to violence."
The complaint adds to mounting pressure on the government over its management of the unrest, with officers arguing that authorities have failed to provide the resources and operational guidance needed to keep demonstrations under control.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said security forces had used crowd-control weapons at least 18,000 times during the protests, primarily smoke and tear gas, but also projectiles and grenades.
One of the weapons was a launcher-fired grenade that produces a deafening blast. Nunez said it had been used about 40 times before he suspended its deployment against high school students after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
The minister defended the use of crowd-control equipment, saying officers deployed it when necessary and in proportion to the threat.
"All this equipment, all these forces, all these intermediate weapons, are used whenever necessary, with proportionality, to mark an escalation of the response, to keep people at a distance or sometimes to put them out of action,” he said.
Nunez maintained that the rules governing the use of projectiles were strict and clearly defined.
"We avoid everything above the neck,” he said.
But investigations into alleged police misconduct have raised questions about whether those safeguards are being followed in practice.
An officer suspected of firing a projectile that partially blinded a 16-year-old was charged this week with aggravated violence.
The case was among 36 investigations into alleged police misconduct reported by Nunez as of Tuesday. Four concerned injuries described as mutilating, while six involved significant injuries. Other investigations involved alleged beatings, insults and suspected sexual assaults, including a case in which an officer was accused of attempting to drown a protester.
France has more than 250,000 police officers and gendarmes, but the scale of its security apparatus has not prevented recurring confrontations between law enforcement and protesters.
Sebastian Roche, a policing specialist at France’s National Center for Scientific Research, said the government’s political assessment of a protest movement often determines how security forces respond.
He pointed to differences in the treatment of high school students and farmers, who have used road blockades, fires and manure dumped on government buildings to press their demands. Farmers wield considerable political influence in France, Roche said, and have sometimes faced a more accommodating response from authorities.
"It’s the political definition of the movement that defines the police response,” he said.
That distinction has fueled criticism that the state applies different standards of force depending on who is protesting and how politically influential the demonstrators are.
Public attitudes toward the police have also shifted, partly because of the constant circulation of videos showing officers confronting demonstrators, Hrar said.
He recalled how police officers were widely praised for their bravery during the terrorist attacks in France in 2015, a period when their role in protecting the public drew broad recognition.
"When you bombard people every single day with images of police intervening with batons, shields and tear gas, you’re inevitably going to create a negative impression,” he said.

articles.title: PM Modi faces Gen Z revolt as anger spills onto India’s streets
articles.summary: Youth-led protests are mounting pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as frustration over unemployment, alleged electoral manipulation and unfulfilled promises fuels demo...
articles.full_text:
Youth-led protests are mounting pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as frustration over unemployment, alleged electoral manipulation and unfulfilled promises fuels demonstrations across the country.
Despite the deployment of tens of thousands of security personnel, young protesters scaled barricades, chanted anti-government slogans and clashed with police during demonstrations in New Delhi and elsewhere last week.
“Long live the revolution,” one protester shouted before police bundled him into a bus.
The independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) says street protests in India this year are on course to reach their highest level in a decade. Analysts say the unrest, coupled with renewed opposition activity, represents Modi’s most serious political challenge since he took office in 2014.
“The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said activist Yogendra Yadav, who has played a leading role in the demonstrations. “I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.”
Modi’s government and his Bharatiya Janata Party declined to comment.
The latest demonstrations have centered on demands for the resignation of Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar over a voter-roll revision that opposition parties and activists allege favors the BJP and has helped it win recent state elections.
The government, the BJP and the Election Commission deny the accusations, with the ruling party attributing its electoral success to Modi’s popularity and economic growth.
But the protests reflect broader dissatisfaction with the government, including frustration over unemployment, examination paper leaks, crimes against women and the influence of wealthy businessmen alleged to have close ties to Modi.
Many young Indians also accuse the government of prioritizing Hindu nationalist politics over jobs and economic opportunities, while raising concerns about violence against religious minorities, particularly Muslims.
“The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who joined protests in the capital.
Raturi said demonstrators were no longer deterred by the prospect of detention or police violence. Police have denied beating protesters and said officers followed established procedures.
The demonstrations have been energized by the Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led movement that grew from online satire into a nationwide campaign in June after India's chief justice likened unemployed people to “cockroaches.”
Activists have used mobile phones and independent YouTube news channels to circulate footage of the protests, gaining audiences despite what critics describe as limited coverage by India's largely pro-government mainstream media.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and left-wing activist Neha Bora have emerged as prominent online voices, while Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi has joined demonstrations alongside tens of thousands of supporters.
The unrest has drawn comparisons with youth-led protests in neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal that brought down governments. However, analysts caution that India's political landscape and Modi's continuing support make direct comparisons difficult.
Employment remains a major source of anger among young people who grew up during Modi's rise to power and expected greater economic opportunity.
Although India has recorded strong economic growth, government figures put overall unemployment slightly above 5%. Unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 reached 9.9% in 2025, according to government data.
Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed, while about one in five graduates aged 25 to 29 remained jobless.
Repeated examination paper leaks have added to the frustration. In May, protests erupted after the government invalidated examinations for admission to national medical colleges following leaked test papers.
Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in New Delhi, said the scandals had deepened young people's distrust of a system they believe is denying them opportunities despite years of study.
“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.
The government, meanwhile, says the economy generated 168.3 million new jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of religious bias, saying his administration serves all Indians.
India's next general election is not due until 2029, but elections in Uttar Pradesh, the country's most populous state, early next year could offer an indication of whether the growing discontent is weakening the BJP's electoral support.
Analysts caution that street protests do not necessarily translate into votes, and the ruling party retains considerable political strength.
“The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago,” said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

articles.title: 4 killed battling flames as Indonesia’s wildfire crisis deepens
articles.summary: Four men have been killed battling wildfires in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park on Indonesia’s Java island, the forestry ministry said Friday, as the country struggles with a mo...
articles.full_text:
Four men have been killed battling wildfires in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park on Indonesia’s Java island, the forestry ministry said Friday, as the country struggles with a months-long wildfire crisis that has blanketed parts of the region in toxic smoke.
The men were overwhelmed by flames Thursday in the park in East Java, according to a ministry statement that provided no further details about the victims.
Two of the men killed were national park officers, while the other two were security guards assisting them, park spokesman Endrip Wahyutama said.
They were trapped by flames and thick smoke. Three died at the scene, while the fourth died later in a hospital, Endrip said.
A volunteer firefighter and a security guard from a nearby hotel who also joined the rescue effort were receiving medical treatment, he said.
The ministry said the incident underscored the risks of firefighting operations.
“This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation,” the ministry said.
The ministry reported a sharp increase in satellite-detected hotspots, which indicate areas of unusually high temperatures but do not necessarily correspond to individual fires.
By Thursday evening, the number of hotspots nationwide had risen to 799, up from 372 a day earlier.
Most were detected in Central Kalimantan, a province on Borneo island, which Indonesia shares with Malaysia and Brunei, followed by southern Sumatra.
“Central Kalimantan recorded the largest increase (in hotspots), so field operations are being strengthened,” the ministry said.
The ministry also expressed concern about fires near Tanjung Puting National Park, an important habitat for endangered orangutans.
Water-bombing and cloud-seeding operations intended to induce rainfall have been hampered by poor visibility caused by smoke from the fires, it added.
Several locations in Sumatra and Kalimantan were experiencing “unhealthy to very unhealthy conditions, even locally hazardous” because of the haze, the ministry said. The smoke had turned the sky orange in some areas.
“If air conditions worsen, people are advised to reduce outdoor activities and wear masks when outside,” the ministry said.

articles.title: Children bear brunt as Ethiopia fighting fuels fears of wider war
articles.summary: Ten-year-old Iyerusalem lies in a hospital bed in northern Ethiopia, her amputated legs propped up by rolled blankets as she struggles with pain and the loss of her older brother,...
articles.full_text:
Ten-year-old Iyerusalem lies in a hospital bed in northern Ethiopia, her amputated legs propped up by rolled blankets as she struggles with pain and the loss of her older brother, who was killed alongside their horse when fighting struck their home.
“I was in our compound with my older brother and our horse when we were hit. My brother and the horse died,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP) from Ayder Comprehensive Specialised Hospital in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region.
Iyerusalem is among dozens of civilians wounded since fighting erupted between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces on Sept. 23, reviving a conflict in a region still scarred by the devastating 2020-22 war.
Federal forces repelled the TPLF offensive and took control of Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 after rebel leaders and fighters abandoned the city.
The fighting has nevertheless left civilians, including children, with severe injuries and families mourning relatives killed in bombardments.
Many wounded people come from remote villages in southern Tigray, hours from medical care along difficult roads affected by fighting and shelling.
Iyerusalem, from Qarsole village in Alamata district, said her amputated legs were causing severe pain.
“If I get medical treatment and can walk again, I want to go back to school,” she said, as her father, Hiluf, watched anxiously.
Nearby, 12-year-old Hana was recovering from severe facial injuries and a broken leg. The explosion that wounded her killed her mother and brother.
“First I heard a loud explosion, and the whole house shook. I was scared and did not even know what had happened. I could not open my eyes or my mouth,” she said.
“The sound of the explosion keeps coming back in my head.”
In another room, Betelhem, 10, was being treated for a broken leg, while her 6-year-old sister, Melet, had suffered a neck injury. Their pregnant mother was killed when heavy artillery struck their home.
“The bomb hit our house directly, all these people have died, but no one is being held responsible. There is no government,” said their father, Haftom, a 39-year-old shopkeeper.
Birhanu Hailemariam, the emergency coordinator at Ayder hospital, said 34 people wounded by heavy artillery, drones, gunfire and explosives had arrived in recent days. Twenty-three were children, and one patient had died.
Medical staff lacked basic equipment and medicines, including anesthesia, he said.
“But we are doing our best to treat everyone,” he said.
Although the latest fighting had not reached the scale of the previous Tigray war, which the African Union (AU) estimates killed about 600,000 people, fear remained pervasive among patients and medical workers.
“Both are hurting people,” another doctor said of the TPLF and federal forces, asking not to be identified.
Families were reluctant to assign blame for attacks. Hiluf said he did not know who had bombarded his village and feared reprisals if he accused either side.
“I do not want to fight with anyone,” he said. “Let there be peace for us.”
Farther north, residents of the border town of Zalambessa say they are caught between Ethiopian and Eritrean troops as the risk of a broader conflict grows.
Eritrea has deployed thousands of troops to northern Tigray to support forces opposing Ethiopia's central government, according to a security source.
“Ethiopian troops are on one side, and Eritrean troops are on the other,” said Selam, 33, whose first name was changed for security reasons.
Eritrean soldiers initially advanced south before drone strikes forced them to retreat into the surrounding mountains, she said. Although the area was no longer seeing active fighting, her home and small shop had been without electricity or water for a week.
“We are caught in the middle and living in deep anxiety,” she said.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported that Ethiopian federal forces had moved heavy weapons toward Zalambessa in recent days. Eyewitnesses reported seeing a substantial convoy of tanks and other heavy weaponry advancing from the south, though AFP could not independently verify the reports.
Residents described deserted streets, closed businesses and growing shortages as blocked roads disrupted supplies.
“Most people only go out to attend church and pray,” said Hadush, 45, who also requested anonymity.
“Now there is no bread,” he said, describing the worsening hardship.
Selam said federal soldiers were preventing residents from traveling to Adigrat, about 30 kilometers (18 miles) south, making it difficult to visit relatives or obtain essential supplies.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel did not respond to AFP questions about the reported presence of Eritrean troops.
The military buildup has raised international concern that the fighting in Tigray could draw the neighboring countries into another war.
On Wednesday, the United States urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to pursue “de-escalation,” calling on all countries to respect their neighbors' sovereignty and territorial integrity and avoid cross-border incursions.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993. The countries fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000 before relations improved in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office and pursued closer ties with Asmara.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the two countries severing ties this month amid the renewed Tigray conflict.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which launched its offensive on Sept. 23. Eritrea alleges that Ethiopia intends to exploit the fighting to invade its territory and seize Assab port on the Red Sea.
The TPLF initially made gains in the Afar region but has since retreated ahead of advancing federal forces, abandoning towns for the surrounding hills.
Federal troops took Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 and subsequently seized several other towns without encountering opposition. The latest reported advance brought government forces to Rama, about 7 kilometers (4 miles) from the Eritrean border, according to two residents.
